strengths: Novel conceptual contribution: Creative application of multicalibration from fairness literature to optimization with predictions; the insight of 'protecting' algorithm-edge events is elegant
Clean modular framework: Separation of multicalibration preprocessing from final algorithm application enables reuse across instances; clean theoretical characterization in Theorem 1
Rigorous theoretical analysis: Sound proofs; Theorem 2's potential function argument elegantly connects predictor MSE to convergence rate
Generality and extensibility: Framework naturally extends to multiple linear optimization problems (best action selection, rejection, matroids), suggesting principled approach
Clear presentation: Well-motivated introduction with intuitive examples; generally accessible writing
weaknesses: Prohibitively high sample complexity: O(n^8/ε^4) worst-case (O(n^8/ε^2) under optimistic assumptions) requires ~10^16 samples for n=100, ε=0.1; comparison to O(n^4/ε^2 log|C|) alternative questions whether modularity justifies 4 additional orders of magnitude; no tightness analysis

Complete absence of empirical validation: No experiments demonstrating practical convergence, sample complexity tightness, real-world applicability, or scenarios justifying the high sample cost relative to alternatives

Limited practical guidance: No principled approach to defining decision class C for applications; no sensitivity analysis; computational complexity of CHECK oracle for large |W| not addressed; MSE = O(ε^2) assumption unjustified

Incremental theoretical contribution: Theorems 1-2 primarily adapt existing multicalibration machinery (Gopalan et al. 2022b); weight class definition (Eq. 3) is problem-specific but underlying analysis is not fundamentally novel
Incomplete baseline comparison: O(n^4/ε^2) alternative mentioned but not formally analyzed; modularity advantage argued informally; missing comparison to other prediction correction methods
Underexplored design choices: Definition of W₁ ∪ W₂ appears somewhat ad-hoc; no discussion of alternative weight families or principles for choosing W in new domains; no lower bounds
